leaderPrimer:
At some point in these five weeks, someone will ask you a doctrinal question that isn't a doctrinal question. It will sound like a question about the fate of people who never believed, and it will be about a father buried two years ago. Nothing in this study matters more than how you handle that moment. The last things are never abstract in a real room. Behind every chair sits a graveside, a child who has walked away, a death by suicide no one mentions, an atheist brother. The doctrine of hell walks into the room wearing the faces of particular people.

So hold to two rules: no flinching, and no gloating. A teacher who softens hell into nothing loses the room's trust on everything else he says about the Bible, and a teacher who handles it with relish reveals something worse. When a skeptic raises the objection, let it be made at full strength and honor it before any answer. Session 3 sets out the traditional view, the conditionalist view, and universalism. Your job is to keep each fairly on the table without pretending the differences are small. Don't settle for the group what faithful Christians have debated with open Bibles. Do say, out loud, that "the Judge of all the earth" will "do what is just" (Genesis 18:25), and that his justice can be trusted further than our guesses.

Keep the study's center where Scripture keeps it. The hope isn't escape to the clouds but resurrection and a renewed creation, a morning the grieving in your room need more than they need a diagram. Hold hope and grief in the same two hands every week. Whoever cries in your group isn't off topic. They are the topic. If grief tips into despair or talk of not wanting to live, don't treat it as a discussion; stay with the person and help them get real help. End every session facing the morning.

faq.q: Is this study going to give me a chart of the end times, the rapture, the millennium, all of it?
faq.a: No, on purpose. This study is about the country we're going to, not the schedule of the trip. It deals with the hope the whole church has confessed together: the resurrection of the body, the new heavens and new earth, what happens when we die, and the hard question of hell. It doesn't take sides on the timing debates that divide believers, because those are secondary to the hope itself and tend to crowd it out. If you came for a timetable, you'll be disappointed. If you came to recover a solid hope, you're in the right place.

faq.q: Does the study think heaven is clouds and harps and floating souls?
faq.a: The opposite. Session 1 is built to clear that picture away. A bodiless soul drifting in the sky forever isn't the Christian hope but a fragment mistaken for the whole, drawn more from paintings, funeral sentiment, and Plato than from Scripture. The Bible promises resurrection: bodies raised on a renewed earth, God coming down to dwell with his people, the new Jerusalem "coming down out of heaven from God" (Revelation 21:2). The movement is downward and earthward. Following N. T. Wright and others, the study trades the postcard for the real country, which is larger, stranger, and far more physical than most of us were taught.

faq.q: Is the resurrection of the body really necessary, or can I just believe my soul goes to heaven?
faq.a: The resurrection of the body is the Christian hope, not an optional extra. In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul says that if Christ hasn't been raised, "your faith is futile," and he offers no fallback to a surviving soul. The idea that we simply float on forever is closer to Greek philosophy than to Scripture, which promises something only God can do: raise the dead. Your soul being with the Lord when you die is real and good, but it's the corridor, not the room. The destination is your body raised, transformed and imperishable, on a healed earth.

faq.q: Does this study believe in hell, and which view does it teach?
faq.a: It treats hell as real and faces it squarely, and it deliberately doesn't force one view on you. Session 3 sets out three positions at their strongest. The traditional view of eternal conscious punishment, the majority view through church history, held by Augustine and the Reformers and defended today by writers like J. I. Packer and Robert Peterson, grounded in the warnings of Jesus. The conditionalist view, argued by Edward Fudge and held tentatively by John Stott, that the finally lost are judged and then cease to exist. And universalism, which the study takes seriously for the beauty of its hope but judges to claim more than Scripture reveals. The study treats the first two as positions faithful Christians hold, and it won't settle that for you in five weeks. What it insists on is the posture: never gloat about hell, and never flinch from it.

faq.q: How can a loving God send anyone to hell? That's the thing I can't get past.
faq.a: Then you're in good company. Many thoughtful people hold hell hardest against God, and the study won't pretend it's easy. Session 3 states the objection at full weight, the disproportion between a finite life and an endless penalty, and refuses to wave it away. Then it sets out how serious Christians have answered: the traditional view that God honors human freedom all the way down and won't drag into his presence those who refused him, and the conditionalist view that the lost are judged and then perish rather than suffering without end. It doesn't hand you a tidy solution. What it offers is this: the One who warned of the dark is the One who went into it himself on the cross, and came out with the scars. The Judge can be trusted even where the answer is withheld.

faq.q: What does the Bible actually say happens the moment I die?
faq.a: More than we usually notice and less than we'd like; session 4 walks through it. The consistent witness is that those who die in Christ are with the Lord at once. Paul speaks of being "away from the body and at home with the Lord" and calls departing to be with Christ "far better." Jesus told the dying thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise." So the dead in Christ aren't gone; they're home, at rest, safe. But this is what theologians call the intermediate state: the corridor, not the room. They aren't yet raised, and they wait, at peace but expectant, for the resurrection morning on the new earth.

faq.q: My grief is overwhelming. Does my sorrow mean my faith is too weak?
faq.a: No. Session 4 cuts that shame off at the root. Paul doesn't tell grieving Christians not to grieve. He tells them not to "grieve as others do who have no hope." Christian grief is real grief, because death is a real wound. Jesus wept at his friend's tomb. Hope doesn't cancel the grief; it changes its color. You weep at a train platform, not a tomb, for someone who has gone ahead, not gone out. C. S. Lewis wrote A Grief Observed in raw anguish after his wife died; his faith didn't spare him the sorrow but carried him through it. Your grief is love with nowhere to go yet, not a failure of belief. If your grief has become despair, or thoughts of not wanting to live, please tell someone you trust and get help now.

faq.q: Isn't all this talk of heaven just escapism that makes Christians useless on earth?
faq.a: That's a fair charge against a false version of the hope, and the study agrees with it there, while showing that it gets the true hope backwards. Session 5 names the faith of the bunker, the believer who won't plant trees because the orchard is doomed, and rejects it, because session 2 showed the earth will be healed, not discarded. A hope of healing produces people who fight for the patient. Someone who knows his body will be raised can't despise his body now, and people who know the earth will be made new can't treat it as a dumping ground. Rightly understood, the hope of resurrection doesn't pull you off the earth. It plants you in it.

faq.q: What is "the long defeat," and why does the study end there?
faq.a: It's Tolkien's phrase for the way history feels to a Christian: a slow erosion, the cause that loses ground, the body that fails, a world that doesn't visibly get better on our watch. The study ends there because that's where most of us live, and a hope that can't speak into it is no use. Against it the study sets what Tolkien called eucatastrophe, the sudden joyful turn when all seems lost, of which the resurrection is the first and the guarantee. We live the long defeat with the courage of people who've read the last page and know it ends with a morning.

faq.q: Why does the study lean on N. T. Wright, C. S. Lewis, and Tolkien so much?
faq.a: Because each recovered something the modern church had let go thin. N. T. Wright, especially in Surprised by Hope, has spent a career recovering the biblical hope of resurrection and new creation, which anchors sessions 1 and 2. C. S. Lewis, in The Great Divorce, A Grief Observed, and the close of Narnia, gave the church pictures of the solidity of the world to come and showed grief held alongside hope. Tolkien gave us the long defeat and eucatastrophe, the shape of a hope that endures the dark and aches for the morning. They're witnesses, not the source; the source is Scripture. But they've helped many people feel the hope and not only agree with it.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't the afterlife just wishful thinking, a comfort for people afraid to die?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study tries to earn the right to answer it by refusing the cheap version. It doesn't promise that this world is fine and you'll float away from it. It faces hell as the hardest objection there is and doesn't pretend the doctrine is easy. It grounds the hope not in a feeling but in a historical claim: an empty tomb and a body that was seen and touched and ate. That's a claim you can investigate, not a warm wish. What the study finally offers isn't a denial of the dark but the claim that Someone has been to the far side of it and come back. You can weigh that. The study doesn't ask you to pretend.

faq.q: How do I lead this if I have my own doubts about the afterlife and my own grief?
faq.a: Your doubt and grief don't disqualify you; they may be your best qualification. The study is built to be led by a fellow traveler, not by someone who has seen the country and come back with a map. Every discussion question has a note behind it, and every session ends in prayer, so you aren't improvising. Being truthful about your own questions, especially about hell, and your own losses can let others stop performing a certainty they don't feel. What you need is to refuse to gloat about hell or flinch from it, keep the room safe for the grieving and the doubting, trade the thin picture of heaven for the solid one gently, and point everyone, yourself first, to the One who has the scars.

timeline.event: Genesis grounds the hope in the goodness of creation: God makes the material world and calls it "very good," a conviction that any picture of salvation as escape from the body must finally reckon with.
The book of Isaiah promises that God will "swallow up death forever" and "wipe away tears from all faces" (Isaiah 25:8), and will create "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17).
Plato, in dialogues such as the Phaedo, describes the body as a prison of the soul and the philosopher's hope as the soul's release, an idea that later seeps into Christian imagination.
Daniel 12:2 promises that "many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake," and by Jesus' day the resurrection of the dead is a settled hope among the Pharisees (Acts 23:8).
Jesus is crucified, buried, and raised bodily on the third day, seen and touched and eating fish to show he isn't a ghost (Luke 24:39-43).
Paul writes 1 Corinthians 15, staking the faith on the bodily resurrection and describing the resurrection body as a seed sown perishable and raised imperishable.
John records Revelation, with its vision of a new heaven and a new earth, the holy city coming down from God, and the One on the throne making all things new.
Origen of Alexandria speculates that all might finally be restored to God, an early root of Christian universalism; the church later rejected his teaching on this point.
Augustine writes The City of God, whose later books defend the eternal punishment of the lost and shape the dominant Western view for more than a thousand years.
Dante completes the Divine Comedy, fixing a vivid picture of hell, purgatory, and paradise in the Western imagination, for better and worse.
C. S. Lewis publishes The Problem of Pain, writing that the doors of hell are locked on the inside.
C. S. Lewis publishes The Great Divorce, picturing the solidity of heaven and the lost who cling freely to their misery.
J. R. R. Tolkien's essay "On Fairy-Stories" is published, coining "eucatastrophe" and calling the resurrection the eucatastrophe of the whole human story.
C. S. Lewis publishes A Grief Observed after his wife's death, refusing to tidy up his anguish.
Edward Fudge publishes The Fire That Consumes, the most sustained modern biblical case for the conditionalist view.
In Essentials, a published dialogue with David Edwards, John Stott says he leans tentatively toward conditionalism.
N. T. Wright publishes Surprised by Hope, urging the church to recover bodily resurrection and the renewal of creation as the Christian hope.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here, and for being willing to look at the hardest and largest things there are: what happens when we die and what God is finally doing with the world. Before we start, three things. First, this is a safe room. You can bring your doubt here. You can say, "I'm not sure I believe any of this." You can bring your grief, fresh or old, and nobody will rush to fix you or tie a bow on it. Second, this study takes the hard things seriously, hell most of all, and it will never gloat about it and never flinch from it. Faithful Christians have landed in different places on some of this, and we aren't here to win arguments but to recover a solid hope. Third, I'm not standing over the doubters and the grieving. Some of us are the doubters and the grieving. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. I'll read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it for a moment before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says. Now let's bring it home, off the page and into the lives we're actually living, into the long defeat and the fresh grief and the ordinary Tuesday, because that's where this hope either matters or doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it isn't all resolved. The last things don't resolve on a schedule, and pretending they do would be a lie. Carry the weight of this toward Jesus this week instead of carrying it alone. Try the practice, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if tonight stirred up grief or doubt that's too heavy to carry by yourself, please tell someone, because this is exactly what the body of Christ is for. Let me pray for us before we go. Thanks for being willing to be truthful tonight.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety, doubt, and grief, and take session 1's opening questions slowly. Say plainly that hell will be handled without gloating or flinching, and that grief will be honored.
Week 2: Session 1, The Wrong Picture, with time on where our inherited picture of heaven came from.
Week 3: Session 2, The Resurrection of the Body, with extra time on "life after life after death" and the renewal of creation.
Week 4: Session 3, Hell, Honestly, part one: the objection at full weight and the traditional view.
Week 5: Session 3 continued: the conditionalist view and universalism, each heard fairly, then the practice and prayer.
Week 6: Session 4, The Dead in Christ, with gentle, unhurried space for grief.
Week 7: Session 5, The Long Defeat and the Final Morning.
Week 8: Bringing it together. Look back over the five practices, talk about what each person is carrying, and make space for anyone wrestling with grief or doubt to be prayed for.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together: the wrong picture cleared away and the resurrection of the body recovered.
Week 2: Session 3, Hell, Honestly, with enough time for all three views to be heard fairly and the objection taken at full weight.
Week 3: Session 4, The Dead in Christ: the intermediate state, the communion of saints, and grief held with hope.
Week 4: Session 5, The Long Defeat and the Final Morning, with a short closing time on living now in light of then.

glossary.definition: The Christian hope that the dead will be raised bodily: the same self transformed and made imperishable, a renewed physical person on a renewed earth, patterned on the risen Christ who was seen and touched and ate.
The biblical promise that God won't discard creation but heal it, setting it free from decay, with his dwelling come down among his people (Isaiah 65:17; Revelation 21:1-3).
N. T. Wright's phrase for the fuller hope beyond the soul's presence with Christ at death: the bodily resurrection on the new earth.
The condition of the dead in Christ between death and resurrection: with the Lord, at rest and safe, yet not yet raised, awaiting the morning when body and soul are joined again.
The creed's confession that the church isn't divided by death but is one body in Christ: the living and the faithful dead joined together in him.

The traditional and historically majority view of hell: the finally lost are consciously and everlastingly separated from God. Grounded in Jesus' warnings and defended by Augustine, the Reformers, and modern writers such as J. I. Packer and Robert Peterson.

Also called annihilationism: immortality is a gift given to the redeemed, not something every soul has by nature, and the finally unrepentant are judged and then cease to exist. Argued by Edward Fudge and held tentatively by John Stott.
The hope that all will finally be saved. This study honors the longing that none be lost but judges that the view claims more than Scripture reveals.
J. R. R. Tolkien's word for the sudden joyful turn at the darkest point of a story. Tolkien called the resurrection the eucatastrophe of the whole human story.
Tolkien's phrase for history as a Christian experiences it: a slow erosion, a cause that loses ground, lived with courage because the final morning lies beyond it.
Paul's image for Christ's resurrection as the first sheaf of a harvest: the guarantee that the bodily raising of all who are his will follow (1 Corinthians 15:20).
The Greek philosophical tradition, from Plato, that treats the body as a prison and salvation as the soul's escape from it, the borrowed idea behind the bodiless picture of heaven.
Revelation's phrase for the final fate of the lost (Revelation 20:14), read by conditionalists as a real ending and by the traditional view as conscious, unending separation.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Many of us were handed a picture of heaven that's mostly clouds and harps, a bodiless forever in the sky, and few of us stop to ask whether the Bible promises anything so thin.
